events.title: Early Human Habitation
events.description: Archaeological evidence shows modern human activity in Eswatini region dating to Late Stone Age. Lion Cavern hematite mining site is one of world's oldest mines, dating back approximately 43,000 years. These early inhabitants used stone tools and engaged in hunter-gatherer activities. Cave paintings and rock art throughout region demonstrate early human cultural activities.

events.title: San (Bushmen) Settlement
events.description: San people (Bushmen) were earliest known inhabitants of region, living as hunter-gatherers in Eswatini's mountains and lowlands for thousands of years. San left rich legacy of rock art depicting animals, hunting scenes and ritual activities. These paintings found in caves and rock shelters throughout country are important resources for studying prehistoric culture. San developed complex ecological knowledge and social structures.

events.title: Bantu Migration Begins
events.description: Bantu-speaking peoples began migrating south from Central and East Africa, gradually entering present-day Eswatini region. These early Bantu migrants brought iron technology, agricultural knowledge and pastoralism. They cultivated crops like sorghum and millet, raised cattle and sheep. Bantu arrival changed region's demographic and lifestyle, gradually replacing or assimilating indigenous San. Iron use greatly increased agricultural productivity.

events.title: Iron Age Culture Development
events.description: Bantu communities consolidated settlement in Eswatini region, developing mature Iron Age culture. Archaeological discoveries show sophisticated iron smelting techniques, pottery making and agricultural practices during this period. Settlement sizes expanded and social stratification began. Cattle's importance in economic and social life increased, becoming symbols of wealth and status. Inhabitants of this period began establishing more permanent villages, developing early clan organizational forms. Trade networks with neighboring regions gradually formed.

events.title: Nguni Settlement
events.description: Nguni-speaking peoples, including ancestors of Swazi, settled in region during this period. They established clan-based social structures, developing unique cultural traditions including age-regiment system, cattle culture and chieftainship. Nguni were primarily pastoralists, with cattle central to social, economic and religious life. They built beehive-shaped grass huts forming kraal settlements. This period laid foundation for Swazi culture.

events.title: Mabudu-vune Settlements
events.description: Archaeological evidence shows complex stone-built settlements within present-day Eswatini, particularly in northern and central regions. These settlements included stone-walled livestock enclosures and residential areas, reflecting advances in social organization. Inhabitants of this period engaged in long-distance trade, connecting with Swahili merchants on East African coast, trading ivory, hides and metal goods. Social stratification became more pronounced, with emergence of early chiefs and noble classes. These developments laid foundations for later kingdom formation.

events.title: Dlamini Dynasty Origins
events.description: According to oral tradition, Swazi royal Dlamini clan origins trace to this period. Legendary ancestor Dlamini I led people migrating from Great Lakes region of East Africa. Dlamini clan initially settled in Tembe River area of present-day southern Mozambique, later gradually migrating west. This clan would become ruling family of Swazi kingdom, continuing over 500 years to present. Dlamini clan's totem is lion.

events.title: Ngwane III Rule
events.description: Ngwane III was important early ruler of Dlamini dynasty. Swazi people named after him as 'Ngwane people' (later evolved to Swazi). He consolidated clan power and expanded territorial control. Ngwane III established more organized political structure, strengthening chief's authority. During his rule, Dlamini clan began emerging from numerous Nguni clans, laying foundation for later unified kingdom.

events.title: Ngwane IV Migration
events.description: Ngwane IV led people migrating west from Tembe River region, crossing Lubombo Mountains into present-day central Eswatini. This migration sought better pastures and escape from conflicts with neighboring clans. Ngwane IV established new settlements in Shiselweni region. This migration marked Swazi establishment in present territory, crucial moment in Swazi nation formation.

events.title: Sobhuza I Rule Begins
events.description: Sobhuza I (Ndvungunye) inherited throne, becoming one of most important rulers in Swazi history. During his reign (c.1780-1839) he unified scattered clans into powerful kingdom. Sobhuza I established centralized political system, created age-regiment military system, strengthened royal power. He was also diplomat, establishing relations with neighboring Zulu and Sotho peoples.

events.title: Mfecane Period
events.description: Mfecane ('crushing' or 'forced migration') was period of massive upheaval and population displacement triggered by Zulu King Shaka's military expansion. Swazi kingdom severely affected, facing pressure from Zulu and other fleeing groups. Sobhuza I adopted flexible diplomatic and military strategies, both resisting aggression and absorbing refugees, enabling kingdom survival and growth. During this period Swazi forced to migrate multiple times, finally settling in present central highlands. Mfecane reshaped entire southern African political landscape.

events.title: Relations with Zulu Kingdom
events.description: Swazi kingdom established complex relationship with powerful Zulu kingdom. Sobhuza I acknowledged Zulu King Shaka's dominance, paying tribute but maintaining considerable autonomy. Swazi sometimes participated in military operations as Zulu allies, sometimes resisted Zulu aggression. This delicate diplomatic balance enabled Swazi kingdom survival under Zulu hegemony. Cultural exchange and intermarriage occurred between kingdoms. Swazi military organization influenced by Zulu system.

events.title: First Contact with Boers
events.description: During Great Trek, Boers (Dutch-descended South Africans) began entering areas near Swazi territory. Swazi first established contact with European colonizers. Initial contact relatively peaceful with trade occurring. But Boer land demands soon created tensions. Sobhuza I cautiously dealt with Boers, trying to balance maintaining independence and avoiding conflict. This marked Swazi kingdom's entry into colonial era.

events.title: Mswati II Accession
events.description: After Sobhuza I's death, following brief succession crisis, his son Mswati II acceded. Mswati II was one of greatest kings in Swazi history; Swazi people and nation named after him. During his reign (1839-1868) he expanded kingdom to maximum extent, north to present Barberton, south to Pongola River. Mswati II strengthened centralization, perfected military system, making Swazi regional power.

events.title: Kingdom Expansion and Peak
events.description: Under Mswati II, Swazi kingdom reached zenith. He conquered surrounding small clans, incorporating them into Swazi nation. Kingdom territory expanded to approximately 200,000 square kilometers, over ten times present Eswatini area. Mswati II built powerful army organized into multiple age-regiments, mobilizing thousands of warriors. He was also shrewd diplomat, establishing relations with Zulu, Boers and British. This period saw full development of Swazi culture and political institutions.

events.title: First Missionary Arrival
events.description: Methodist missionary James Allison became first Christian missionary entering Swaziland. He established mission station with Mswati II's permission. Though initial converts few, this marked beginning of Christianity spread in Swaziland. Missionaries brought Western education and medicine, profoundly impacting Swazi society. Mswati II open to missionaries but insisted on maintaining traditional culture and religion. Missionary activity accelerated under later rulers.

events.title: Increased Contact with European Explorers
events.description: During 1850s, increasing numbers of European explorers, hunters and traders entered Swaziland. These included famous explorers like Thomas Baines, who documented Swazi lifestyle and kingdom's prosperity. These contacts brought trade in firearms, horses and other European goods. Mswati II skillfully used these relationships to strengthen kingdom's military power and economic position. But this also opened prelude to European influence penetration, laying groundwork for later colonial era.

events.title: Gold Discovery and Concessions Crisis Begins
events.description: Gold and other minerals discovered in Swazi territory attracted numerous European prospectors and speculators. Mswati II and later rulers began granting Europeans mining, grazing and commercial concessions in exchange for money, weapons and protection promises. But kings often didn't understand legal implications of these concessions, leading to massive land and resource control by foreigners. These concessions later became major threat to Swazi sovereignty, nearly causing kingdom's demise.

events.title: Mbandzeni Accession
events.description: Mswati II died, his son Mbandzeni acceded after regency period, formally in 1875. Mbandzeni's rule (1875-1889) was period when Swazi kingdom faced serious external pressures. He inherited powerful kingdom beginning to face European colonialism threats. Mbandzeni tried maintaining independence through diplomacy but made fatal errors on concessions, granting excessive rights to Europeans.

events.title: Concessions Flood
events.description: During Mbandzeni's rule, Swaziland fell into 'concessions mania.' King granted hundreds of Europeans mining, land, grazing, trade concessions, often overlapping and contradictory. By Mbandzeni's death in 1889, virtually entire country covered by concessions. These concession holders mainly Boers and British, also competing for control. Swazi kingdom's sovereignty and territorial integrity seriously threatened. Traditional land ownership and political authority undermined. This period viewed as disaster in Swazi history.

events.title: First Boer War Impact
events.description: In First Boer War (1880-1881), Transvaal defeated British, regaining independence as South African Republic. This outcome significantly impacted Swaziland as Boer power strengthened, and their territorial ambitions toward Swaziland grew. Mbandzeni forced to navigate between Boers and British, attempting to use their competition to preserve kingdom's independence. However, this diplomatic balancing became increasingly difficult, and Swaziland's autonomy continuously eroded.

events.title: Swazi Capital Relocation
events.description: Due to European pressure and seeking safer location, Swazi royal family relocated main residence to area near Ezulwini Valley. This region provided better defensive position and fertile land. However, with spread of concessions, even royal traditional lands no longer secure. This relocation reflected Swazi royal power's vulnerability under European colonial pressure. Ezulwini Valley later became Swaziland's cultural and political center.

events.title: Provisional Government Established
events.description: After Mbandzeni's death, due to concessions chaos and European pressure, under Boer South African Republic (Transvaal) domination, provisional government established comprising Europeans and Swazi. This government attempted sorting concessions chaos but actually weakened Swazi royal power. Young King Bhunu and Regent Labotsibeni's power limited. This marked Swaziland beginning to lose actual independence.

events.title: Transvaal Protectorate
events.description: Under Swaziland Convention, Boer South African Republic (Transvaal) gained protection rights and actual control over Swaziland, though nominally Swaziland remained independent. Transvaal established special commissioner in Swaziland, controlling foreign affairs and internal matters. Swazi king's power further weakened, becoming symbolic. Many Swazi dissatisfied with arrangement but powerless to resist. During this period many Boer immigrants entered Swaziland, acquiring land.

events.title: King Bhunu's Death
events.description: Young King Bhunu died after ruling only ten years, aged 23. During his reign royal power severely weakened, virtually powerless against European colonial pressure. When Bhunu died, his son Sobhuza (later Sobhuza II) only months old. Queen Mother Labotsibeni Gwamile became regent, playing crucial role over following decades, leading Swazi through most difficult colonial period.

events.title: Boer War Impact
events.description: During Second Boer War (South African War), Swaziland became battlefield. Both British and Boers tried gaining Swazi support. Regent Labotsibeni adopted neutral stance, but Swaziland still suffered war destruction. After war ended, British defeated Boers, Swaziland's fate in British hands. Swazi hoped British would restore their independence and land, but these hopes soon dashed.

events.title: British Protectorate Established
events.description: After Boer War ended, British took control of Swaziland, placing it under Transvaal Colony Governor's jurisdiction. In 1906, Swaziland formally became British protectorate, ruled by High Commissioner. Swazi king retained symbolic status but real power held by British colonial officials. British recognized most Boer land concessions, causing Swazi to lose approximately two-thirds of traditional land. This triggered decades-long Swazi land recovery struggle.

events.title: Land Partition
events.description: British colonial authorities implemented land partition, dividing Swaziland into European-owned private land and Swazi 'native areas.' Approximately two-thirds of land allocated to Europeans (mainly Boers), Swazi restricted to poorer reserves. This land partition destroyed traditional land use patterns, causing serious social and economic problems. Many Swazi became tenants or laborers on European farms. Land issue became core of Swazi nationalism.

events.title: Impact of Union of South Africa Formation
events.description: After Union of South Africa formed, Swaziland faced pressure for incorporation. Union of South Africa Act originally included provisions to incorporate Swaziland, Basutoland (Lesotho) and Bechuanaland (Botswana). But due to British hesitation and local opposition, Swaziland ultimately remained independent British protectorate. However, Swaziland's economic and administrative ties with South Africa deepened, with South Africa becoming main destination for Swazi migrant laborers. This decision profoundly impacted Swaziland's future development.

events.title: During World War I
events.description: During World War I, though Swaziland not directly involved in combat, war impacted region. Some Swazi served British as laborers or military auxiliaries. War caused trade disruptions and price increases, affecting local economy. Regent Labotsibeni used this period to strengthen traditional authority, continuing to advocate for young Sobhuza II's rights. Post-war, global political landscape changes and rise of self-determination ideals planted seeds for Swaziland's future nationalist movement.

events.title: Sobhuza II Formal Accession
events.description: After 22-year regency, Sobhuza II formally acceded at age 22, becoming Swaziland king. Sobhuza II would become one of 20th century's longest-reigning monarchs, ruling 61 years (1921-1982). He inherited colonially-ruled kingdom with land dispossessed, but would lead Swazi toward independence and revival. Sobhuza II Western-educated but firmly maintained Swazi traditional culture. His accession ceremony followed traditional customs, lasting months.

events.title: Land Litigation Failure
events.description: Sobhuza II filed lawsuit with British Privy Council challenging 1907 land partition legality, demanding return of Swazi land. This was first time Swazi used legal means fighting for rights. But 1926 Privy Council ruled against Swazi, upholding existing land allocation. This failure made Sobhuza II realize must adopt other strategies. He began gradually recovering lost land through purchasing, while strengthening traditional political structures, preparing for future independence struggle.

events.title: Gradual Land Repurchase
events.description: Sobhuza II launched long-term plan to gradually recover Swazi national land by raising funds to purchase European-owned land. He established Swazi National Fund, mobilizing all Swazi to donate. Though progress slow, by 1960s Swazi had repurchased considerable land. This strategy demonstrated Sobhuza II's patience and strategic vision. Land recovery became symbol of national unity, strengthening royal legitimacy.

events.title: World War II Impact
events.description: During World War II, Swaziland as British protectorate indirectly involved in war. Approximately 3,000 Swazi volunteered for British forces, serving in North Africa and other theaters. War stimulated demand for Swazi agricultural products and minerals, bringing short-term economic prosperity. But war also caused material shortages and inflation. Sobhuza II used wartime cooperation with Britain to enhance royal status. Post-war, rise of decolonization ideals created favorable environment for Swaziland's independence movement.

events.title: Economic Development and Modernization
events.description: After World War II, Swaziland began economic modernization. Colonial government invested in infrastructure including roads, railways and irrigation systems. Commercial agriculture (especially sugar, citrus and forestry) developed, mainly operated by European companies. Mining industry (asbestos, iron ore) also expanded. These developments brought economic growth but benefits mainly flowed to Europeans and colonial government. Swazi mainly participated as laborers, many forced to work in South African mines. Urbanization began, Mbabane developed as administrative center.

events.title: Education and Social Change
events.description: 1950s saw significant expansion of Swaziland's education system, mainly driven by mission schools. Increasing numbers of young Swazi received Western education, forming educated elite class. Sobhuza II encouraged educational development but also worried about westernization's erosion of traditional culture. This period saw emergence of early nationalist intellectuals questioning colonial rule and demanding more political rights. Tensions between tradition and modernization became increasingly apparent, laying foundation for 1960s political changes.

events.title: Decolonization Wave Begins
events.description: In 1960s, African continent saw decolonization wave, many British colonies gained independence. Swaziland also began process toward independence. Sobhuza II and Swazi elite began negotiating constitutional reform and self-government with Britain. But Swaziland's situation complex due to tensions between traditional monarchy, European settler interests and emerging modern political forces. Sobhuza II insisted on maintaining monarchy and traditional authority after independence.

events.title: First Legislative Elections
events.description: Swaziland held first legislative elections, establishing Legislative Council. Sobhuza II-supported Imbokodvo National Movement won overwhelming victory, gaining all seats. This conservative party supported monarchy and traditional values. Progressive opposition like Swaziland Progressive Party marginalized. Election results showed Sobhuza II and traditional authority's strong influence in Swazi society. This laid foundation for post-independence political landscape.

events.title: Internal Self-Government
events.description: Britain granted Swaziland internal self-government status, establishing responsible government. Sobhuza II became head of state, Prince Makhosini became Prime Minister. Swaziland gained all powers except foreign affairs and defense. New constitution balanced traditional authority and modern democratic institutions, establishing bicameral parliament. This was important step toward full independence. Swaziland began building own government institutions and civil service.

events.title: Swaziland Independence
events.description: Swaziland formally gained independence from Britain, becoming sovereign state with Sobhuza II as King. Independence Day celebrations held in Mbabane, British royal representatives attended. Swaziland joined United Nations and Commonwealth. Independence constitution established constitutional monarchy with king having considerable powers. Swaziland one of few African countries retaining traditional monarchy. At independence, Swaziland faced challenges including economic dependence on South Africa and unresolved land issues, but national pride high.

events.title: Economic Growth and South African Relations
events.description: 1970s saw rapid economic growth in Swaziland, mainly relying on sugar, timber, asbestos exports and South African investment. Swaziland maintained close economic relations with apartheid South Africa, joining Southern African Customs Union. This relationship brought economic benefits but also drew criticism from other African countries. Swaziland allowed South African ANC exiles to operate within borders, trying to balance economic interests and African solidarity. Infrastructure improved, education and healthcare expanded.

events.title: Constitution Abolished and Royal Power Strengthened
events.description: Sobhuza II abolished 1968 independence constitution on grounds it was 'unsuitable for Swazi tradition,' dissolved parliament, banned political parties. King declared all power vested in himself and traditional Tinkhundla system. This coup-like action transformed Swaziland from constitutional monarchy to absolute monarchy. Sobhuza II claimed this was to preserve Swazi culture and unity, but critics saw it as authoritarian rule. Thereafter Swaziland became one of Africa's last absolute monarchies.

events.title: New Constitution and Tinkhundla System
events.description: Sobhuza II promulgated new constitution, formally establishing Tinkhundla electoral system. This system based on traditional local councils, voters elect representatives in local constituencies, then indirectly elect parliament members. Political parties banned, candidates run as individuals. King retained power to appoint some MPs and all cabinet members. Critics saw this system as pseudo-democracy, actually consolidating royal power. But supporters claimed it conformed to Swazi tradition, avoiding divisive party politics.

events.title: Sobhuza II's Death
events.description: Sobhuza II died after 61-year reign, aged 83, then world's longest-reigning monarch. His death triggered succession crisis and political turmoil in Swaziland. Sobhuza II left complex legacy: he led Swaziland to independence, preserved traditional culture and monarchy, but also established authoritarian rule. He had over 70 wives and 200+ children. His funeral followed traditional customs, lasting months with national mourning.

events.title: Succession Crisis and Regency Chaos
events.description: After Sobhuza II's death, Queen Mother Dzeliwe appointed regent but replaced by another Queen Mother Ntombi in 1983. This period filled with palace intrigue, power struggles and political instability. Traditional Council (Liqoqo) tried controlling government, conflicting with regent and prime minister. Some princes and politicians arrested or exiled. This crisis exposed Swazi political system's fragility and contradictions within traditional power structures. Young Crown Prince Makhosetive educated in Britain, awaiting accession.

events.title: Mswati III Accession
events.description: 18-year-old Prince Makhosetive acceded as King Mswati III, one of world's youngest monarchs. Accession ceremony followed traditional customs, lasting months. Mswati III inherited nation that experienced four years of turmoil. He quickly consolidated power, dissolved Traditional Council trying to control him, appointed trusted advisors. Mswati III promised continuing father's policies, maintaining tradition and monarchy. His reign would continue to present, over 35 years.

events.title: Democratization Pressure
events.description: With Cold War ending and South African apartheid collapsing, Swaziland faced increasing democratization pressure. Trade unions, students and intellectuals demanded multi-party democracy, new constitution and limited royal power. Early 1990s saw multiple strikes and demonstrations. Mswati III initially refused reforms but under pressure agreed to review constitution. However, reform process slow and controlled by royalty. South Africa's democratic transition made Swaziland's absolute monarchy more isolated.

events.title: Trade Union Movement and Strikes
events.description: Swaziland Federation of Trade Unions (SFTU) led large-scale strikes and demonstrations demanding democratic reforms and workers' rights. Government suppressed with force, arresting union leaders. This marked radicalization of Swaziland's democracy movement. Unions became main force opposing royal power, allying with students, teachers and civil society organizations. Government accused unions of foreign manipulation, attempting to overthrow monarchy. Political tensions escalated but Mswati III refused substantial reforms.

events.title: Constitutional Review Commission
events.description: Under continued pressure, Mswati III appointed Constitutional Review Commission to draft new constitution. Commission conducted nationwide consultations, gathering public opinion. But critics noted commission appointed by king, lacking independence. Democrats demanded constituent assembly and referendum but were refused. Constitution drafting process lasted years, filled with controversy. Many democrats boycotted process, seeing it as royalty's tool to maintain power.

events.title: HIV/AIDS Crisis
events.description: Swaziland suffered one of world's worst HIV/AIDS epidemics, adult infection rate once exceeding 40%, globally highest. Epidemic caused massive deaths, reduced life expectancy, created many orphans, seriously impacting economy and society. Government initially slow to respond, some Mswati III statements controversial. Later under international pressure and aid, government strengthened prevention efforts, providing free antiretroviral treatment. But HIV/AIDS remains Swaziland's most serious public health and development challenge.

events.title: New Constitution Promulgated
events.description: After years of controversy, Mswati III promulgated new constitution, Swaziland's first since 1973. Constitution included Bill of Rights, guaranteeing freedoms of speech, assembly etc. But constitution maintained king's absolute power: king is head of state and executive, appoints prime minister and cabinet, can dissolve parliament, has legislative veto. Political parties still banned. Democrats criticized constitution as 'rubber stamp,' not substantially changing power structure. But government claimed constitution was progress, balancing tradition and modernity.

events.title: Reed Dance Controversy
events.description: Mswati III chose 13th wife at traditional Umhlanga (Reed Dance) ceremony, drawing international criticism. The woman was only 17, reportedly chosen during king's declared 'maiden chastity' period, violating king's own rule. This incident highlighted conflict between traditional customs and modern human rights standards. Critics accused king's lavish lifestyle contrasting sharply with most Swazi's poverty. Reed Dance is important Swazi cultural tradition but also raises gender equality controversies.

events.title: Economic Crisis Begins
events.description: Global financial crisis severely hit Swaziland economy. Southern African Customs Union (SACU) revenue sharply declined, main source of Swaziland government revenue. Exports fell, unemployment rose. Government faced serious fiscal crisis, struggling to pay civil servants and provide basic services. IMF and other institutions provided aid but demanded fiscal reforms and spending cuts. But royal lavish spending continued, causing public anger. Economic difficulties intensified political discontent.

events.title: Fiscal Crisis and Protests
events.description: Swaziland fell into serious fiscal crisis, government nearly bankrupt, unable to pay salaries. Inspired by Arab Spring, democracy activists organized series of protests and strikes, demanding democratic reforms and king's abdication. April 12 declared 'Uprising Day' but large-scale protests suppressed by security forces. Government arrested activists, banned democracy organizations. South Africa provided emergency loan helping Swaziland through crisis but demanded reforms. However, substantial political reforms didn't occur.

events.title: Human Rights Lawyer Persecution
events.description: Prominent human rights lawyer and democracy activist Thulani Maseko and journalist Bheki Makhubu arrested and sentenced for criticizing judicial system, drawing international condemnation. This highlighted Swaziland's lack of freedom of speech and judicial independence. International human rights organizations criticized Swaziland's human rights record, including harassment of activists, arbitrary arrests and torture allegations. Government denied human rights violations, claiming to maintain law and order.

events.title: Elections and Continued Authoritarianism
events.description: Swaziland held parliamentary elections but under party-banned Tinkhundla system. Democrats boycotted elections, turnout low. King-appointed candidates dominated parliament. After elections, Mswati III appointed own son as prime minister candidate, drawing nepotism criticism. International observers criticized elections lacking freedom and fairness. Swaziland's political system basically unchanged, royal power remained absolute.

events.title: Drought and Food Crisis
events.description: Swaziland suffered severe drought, part of climate change impacts. Agricultural production sharply declined, hundreds of thousands faced food insecurity. Government declared national emergency, seeking international aid. Drought exposed Swaziland economy's fragility and dependence on agriculture. Poverty rates rose, especially in rural areas. Critics noted if government resources not wasted on royal lavish spending, nation would be better able to respond to crisis.

events.title: Country Renamed to Eswatini
events.description: At 50th independence anniversary celebrations, Mswati III announced country name change from 'Swaziland' to 'Kingdom of Eswatini,' using siSwati language name. King stated this was to remove colonial legacy, use indigenous name. 'Eswatini' means 'land of the Swazi' in siSwati. This decision made without public consultation or parliamentary approval, drawing some criticism. But many Swazi supported using indigenous name. International community gradually accepted new name.

events.title: Continued Economic Difficulties
events.description: Eswatini continued facing serious economic challenges: high unemployment (especially youth unemployment exceeding 40%), poverty rate around 60%, severe income inequality (Gini coefficient among world's highest). Economy highly dependent on South Africa and SACU revenue. Sugar industry (main export) faced EU market access problems. HIV/AIDS continued affecting workforce. Government debt increased. But royalty continued lavish spending, Mswati III purchasing luxury cars for wives and building palaces, causing public anger.

events.title: COVID-19 Pandemic Impact
events.description: COVID-19 pandemic severely hit Eswatini economy and society. Government implemented lockdown measures but enforcement harsh, security forces accused of excessive force. Economy further deteriorated, many lost livelihoods. Healthcare system overwhelmed. Pandemic exposed Eswatini public health system weaknesses and social inequality. Government's pandemic response capacity questioned. But royalty continued lavish lifestyle, contrasting with people's suffering, intensifying social discontent.

events.title: Democracy Uprising and Crackdown
events.description: Eswatini erupted in largest pro-democracy protests in decades. Triggered by police killing of law student and long-accumulated grievances. Tens of thousands took to streets demanding democratic reforms, elected prime minister and limited royal power. Protests turned violent, demonstrators burned royal-linked businesses and government buildings. Security forces cracked down with live ammunition, causing at least 80 deaths (official figures lower), hundreds injured, thousands arrested. International community condemned violence, Southern African Development Community (SADC) intervened to mediate. But Mswati III refused substantial reforms, calling protests 'terrorism.'

events.title: Continued Repression and International Pressure
events.description: After 2021 uprising, Eswatini government intensified repression. Security forces continued harassing and arresting activists. Many democracy leaders exiled. Government charged protesters with terrorism and sedition. Judicial system used to persecute dissidents. International human rights organizations documented widespread abuses including torture, enforced disappearances and extrajudicial killings. US removed Eswatini from African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA) trade preferences citing human rights violations. SADC tried promoting dialogue but progress limited.

events.title: Human Rights Lawyer Thulani Maseko Assassinated
events.description: Prominent human rights lawyer and democracy activist Thulani Maseko shot dead at home by unidentified gunmen. Maseko was leading figure in Eswatini democracy movement, long-time critic of royal power and human rights advocate. His assassination drew international shock and condemnation. Many suspected political assassination but government denied involvement. Maseko's funeral became democracy movement rally, thousands attended. His death symbolized danger of Eswatini's democratic struggle and government repression's brutality. International community demanded independent investigation but no one brought to justice yet.

events.title: Economic Sanctions and Isolation
events.description: Due to deteriorating human rights record, Eswatini faced increasing international pressure and sanctions. US continued excluding it from AGOA, affecting textile exports. EU and other international partners cut aid or attached human rights conditions. Eswatini increasingly isolated internationally. But government refused reforms, accusing foreign interference in internal affairs. Economic difficulties intensified but royal lifestyle unchanged. Democracy movement continued but faced harsh repression. Eswatini became one of Africa's most repressive countries.

events.title: Africa's Last Absolute Monarchy
events.description: Eswatini remains sub-Saharan Africa's only absolute monarchy. Mswati III ruling nearly 40 years with unchecked power. He has 15 wives, lives extremely lavish lifestyle while approximately 70% of population lives below poverty line. Political freedoms severely restricted: parties banned, speech and assembly freedoms suppressed, judiciary not independent, security forces violate human rights. Economy dependent on South Africa, facing high unemployment, HIV/AIDS epidemic and climate change impacts. Democracy movement continues resisting but faces brutal repression. International community applies pressure but reform prospects bleak. Eswatini's future full of uncertainty: will authoritarian rule continue or will democratic transition eventually occur? Younger generation increasingly dissatisfied, demanding change. But Mswati III seems determined to maintain royal power, willing to use violence. Eswatini epitomizes 21st century conflict between absolute monarchy and democratic aspirations, its development will affect entire southern African region's stability.
